newsitem.title: USA: Bulk of suicide cult members bodies being sent home.
newsitem.headline: Bulk of suicide cult members bodies being sent home.

text.p: Authorities released more of the bodies of 39 Heaven's Gate cult members on Monday as investigators searched for answers to the bizzare mass suicide.

The bodies were discovered in a $1.6-million mansion in the exclusive San Diego suburb of Rancho Santa Fe last Wednesday but county Medical Examiner Brian Blackbourne said he believed the members died in batches, possibly starting as early as the previous Saturday. The group, which designed computer web sites, believed they would be transported to heaven by a UFO hiding behind the Hale-Bopp comet.
"We are releasing the bodies as we speak," Calvin Vine of the San Diego County Medical examiner's office said. "Probably most of them will be released later in the day."

On Sunday, former cult members tried to explain what drew them to leave their families and follow the group's telegenic leader, Marshall Herff Applewhite. Wayne Cooke, whose wife Suzanne Sylvia Cooke was one of the 39, said on the CBS "60 Minutes" programme he wished he had had the courage to follow suit.

"I think she's probably on another (space) craft somewhere out there," Cooke said of his wife, who like other Heaven's Gate cultists ate drug-laced pudding or applesauce, washed it down with vodka and put a plastic bag over her head to die.

"I wish I had the strength to have remained to have gained the kind of control through Do's help, and Ti's help, to have stuck it out and gotten stronger and continued to be a part of that crew," Cooke said.
"Do" was the cult name for Applewhite, who with partner "Ti" -- a nurse who died in 1985 -- came up with the theory that the group's spirits would be picked up by a spaceship.

Both Cooke, who said he joined and left Heaven's Gate several times, and another former member identified only as "Sawyer" also interviewed on "60 Minutes" had nothing but good words for a cult whose deaths have shocked the world.

Sawyer said he once believed in Applewhite's message of renouncing human ties and corporeal distractions to the point that he considered emulating the former music teacher and voluntarily castrating himself.
"I wanted to very badly at the time," said Sawyer, who eventually opted against the procedure. "I flipped a coin, I lost -- as far as the castration (goes)."

In San Diego, investigators sorted through hundreds of computer files left behind by the group in the hope of learning more about the reasons behind the bizarre deaths. According to several reports, Applewhite may have lied about his health, telling some followers he was dying of cancer.
Vine said Applewhite's autopsy showed no signs of cancer, and other officials have noted that none of the cult members mentioned his alleged cancer in their suicide videotapes.

Also appearing on "Today," Nick Mitzorkis, a Beverly Hills computer consultant whose employee made the grizzly discovery on Wednesday, said two computer floppy disks were sent to the employee, named only as Rio and identified as a fomer member of the cult, by the group along with the videotapes.
He said members of the cult had put their suicide notes on the disks as well as on video.

Two businessmen are interested in buying the mansion and have discussed tearing it down "to bring closure to the whole negative event," Robert Dyson, owner and president of Dyson and Dyson Real Estate in Rancho Sante Fe, said. He said he brought the two together because they had similar intentions.
"We're waiting to see what they will do," he said. While no firm offers have been made, "part of the discussion was possibly tearing down this house and starting over again."
